name: Georgian
confidence_why: Two independent instrumental studies, Jun, Vicenik and Lofstedt (2007) and Borise (2023, with Borise and Zientarski 2018), find fixed initial stress cued by duration and show the antepenultimate prominence of the older textbook rule (Robins and Waterson 1952, Aronson 1990, still assumed by Skopeteas and Féry 2016) to be a phrasal pitch target, so initial stress is the likely answer even though Georgian stress is acoustically weak and the older account has not disappeared.
catalog_quote: F0-marking in Georgian is reserved for phrasal prosody and is not intrinsic to stress-marking.
sweep_summary: Georgian (nucl1302) is in the catalog as fixed-dominant with Gordon 2002's antepenultimate rule string and an F0-only deciding quote from Borise 2023's abstract. Of the 9 title-works with stress in the title (8 distinct works; 558189 = 591138), 6 were read in full: Borise & Zientarski 2018 (held by the project) and Borise 2021 Glossa (Internet Archive copy; publisher site behind Anubis) state fixed initial, duration-cued stress; Skopeteas & Féry 2016 (draft recovered from an Internet Archive copy of Bielefeld PUB) adopts the textbook rule 'initial in 2-3 syllable words, antepenult primary + initial secondary in longer words', i.e. the catalog's own pattern, but calls it tentative and postlexical; Borise 2017 (Cascadilla, open) and Skopeteas & Féry 2014 (the Internet Archive/PUB) are focus-prosody papers that only report the debate. Vicenik & Jun 2014 (OUP) and Skopeteas, Féry & Asatiani 2018 (Benjamins) are closed; Crossref abstracts obtained (Vicenik & Jun: antepenult H tones are an Accentual-Phrase property, not word stress). Zhgenti 1964 (STUF, De Gruyter) is closed with no abstract reachable; medium priority since Borise 2023 already summarizes Zhghenti's experiments. Best statement: Borise 2023 PDA 5(1) §6 p. 32 - initial word-level stress, no evidence for antepenultimate stress - which supersedes the Gordon/Zhgenti antepenult rule while confirming the fixed, weight-insensitive kind. Bonus: Borise's lingbuzz survey chapter (004204, §3.2) catalogs every older Georgian stress account.

new_statements.quote: If viewed against the backdrop of the existing literature, which allowed us to hypothesize that Georgian stress may be initial, penultimate, or antepenultimate, the current results demonstrate that Georgian has initial word-level stress, while the penult houses a phrasal tonal target. Notably, the results provide no evidence for antepenultimate stress. This is consistent with Alkahzishvili (1959: 402), who, similarly, found no acoustic evidence for antepenultimate stress.
new_statements.citation: Borise, Lena. 2023. Disentangling word stress and phrasal prosody: A view from Georgian. Phonological Data & Analysis 5(1), Article 1: 1-37. doi:10.3765/pda.v5art1.43 (CC BY 3.0).
new_statements.locator: §6 Discussion, p. 32 (cf. abstract p. 1: 'this finding provides evidence in favor of fixed initial stress'; §7 Conclusion p. 32)
new_statements.reading: Fixed initial word stress, cued by syllable duration (possibly intensity), insensitive to syllable count and phrasal context; the penult and antepenult carry only phrasal F0 targets, not stress. This is the first-hand instrumental result, corroborated independently by Borise & Zientarski 2018 (TAL) and, second-hand, by Vicenik & Jun 2014: 156. It keeps Georgian in the fixed / weight-insensitive (dominant) class but places stress on the initial syllable in words of every length, so the catalog's Gordon-2002 stress placement coded per word length as 100 0100 10100 100100 1000100 10000100 (1 = a stressed syllable) (antepenultimate primary, initial secondary) should be replaced by initial stress (initial stress). The older antepenult accounts survive only as textbook rules of thumb (Skopeteas & Féry 2016 §2.2, citing Robins & Waterson 1952 and Aronson 1990: 18).

new_statements.quote: The first syllable of an AP is often prominent by having stronger amplitude and longer duration (though not as prominent as stress in English). This suggests that the first syllable of a word is stressed in Georgian, as proposed by Robin and Waterson (1952) and Aronson (1990), mentioned above. However, the antepenultimate syllable of a word did not show stronger amplitude or longer duration. Instead, it sometimes showed a high tone, immediately followed by a low tone on the penultimate syllable. [...] This suggests that the antepenultimate syllable of a word is not stressed at the lexical level.
new_statements.citation: Jun, Sun-Ah and Vicenik, Chad and Lofstedt, Ingvar (2006). Intonational phonology of Georgian. UCLA Working Papers in Phonetics 106. pp. 41–57.
new_statements.locator: §1 Introduction pp. 41-42 (survey of Robins & Waterson 1952 and Aronson 1990 rules); §3 Results pp. 42-43 (deciding passage); §4 Discussion and Summary pp. 54-55
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File (18 PDF pages; eScholarship cover + pp. 41-57). The quoted passage is verbatim at §3 Results, p. 42 bottom to p. 43 top (the text), including the paper's own spelling 'Robin and Waterson (1952)'; the bracketed ellipsis skips three sentences about the HL fall crossing word boundaries. p. 43 also says 'Georgian has a pitch accent linked to the stressed syllable of a word.. An AP can have more than one word, but only the first stressed syllable is realized with a pitch accent'; p. 44 (Fig. 2 text) 'The pitch accented, initial-syllable nuclear [a]-sounds in [mananam] and [dabana] are longer and their amplitudes are greater than those of the [a]-sounds in non-initial syllables'; §4 pp. 54-5…
new_statements.relation_note: Contradicts the catalog's Gordon record (stress placement coded per word length as 100 0100 10100 100100 1000100 10000100 (1 = a stressed syllable) = antepenultimate primary with initial secondary): Jun et al. find the antepenult carries no stress, only a phrasal H+L tone, and word stress is initial. Agrees with the existing Borise 2023 statement (fixed initial stress, penult/antepenult F0 targets are phrasal) and is in fact its earlier instrumental precursor (Borise cites Vicenik & Jun 2014 for the same finding).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the first syllable (greater amplitude and duration, weaker than English stress); a post-lexical pitch accent (L*, H*, L*+H or L+H*) is linked to that initial stressed syllable of the Accentual Phrase. The high pitch on the antepenult that earlier work took for (primary) antepenultimate stress is analysed as an H+L phrase accent on the antepenult-penult of the Accentual Phrase, not a property of the word: p. 55 'Observations of pitch at a sentence level, however, suggest that the high pitch on the antepenultimate syllable is not a property of a word, but of a phrase, AP. The high pitch was on the antepenult of an AP regardless of its location in a word.'
new_statements.secondary_stress: None claimed. The paper explicitly denies lexical antepenultimate stress (the '1st & antepenult' pattern of Robins & Waterson 1952 and Aronson 1990 for words of 5+ syllables, tabulated in (1)-(2) on p. 41) and replaces the antepenult prominence with a phrasal H+L accent; it does not posit any secondary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: The H+L phrase accent appears mainly in yes/no questions, wh-questions and focus phrases; it can straddle a word boundary when two words share an AP (p. 43, p. 51 Figure 8). Only the first stressed syllable of a multi-word AP carries a pitch accent (p. 43). Four speakers (3 female, 1 male) of standard Georgian recorded at UCLA; word-list prominence measurements are impressionistic, not quantified.
new_statements.identity_note: Jun et al. 2007 describe standard Georgian as spoken by four adult speakers (three female, one male, in their 30s-40s) recorded at UCLA in 2007; no dialect is named. Gvantseladze 2003 (not opened) has an Abkhaz-language title and is a bilingual Georgian-Abkhaz grammar, so any stress statement in it might concern Abkhaz as well as Georgian.

readall_conflicts: The catalog's Gordon record codes Georgian with antepenultimate primary stress and initial secondary stress (stress placement coded per word length as 100 0100 10100 100100 1000100 10000100 (1 = a stressed syllable)), following the Robins & Waterson 1952 / Aronson 1990 rules of thumb. Jun, Vicenik & Lofstedt 2007 (pp. 42-43, 54-55) reject the antepenult stress on instrumental grounds: the antepenult shows no extra amplitude or duration, and its high pitch is an H+L phrase accent of the Accentual Phrase that sits on the antepenult of the phrase regardless of word boundaries, while the word-initial syllable is the one with greater amplitude and duration and carries the pitch accent. This is the same conclusion as the existing Borise 2023 statement (fixed initial word stress; penult/antepenult F0 targets are phrasal), so the two opened-and-relevant sources for this language agree with each other and jointly contradict the catalog record. Goldstein, Chitoran & Selkirk 2007 is silent; Gvantseladze 2003 and Ritter 2006 could not be opened. 32: 'the current results demonstrate that Georgian has initial word-level stress, while the penult houses a phrasal tonal target', re-verified in line 1494), corroborated by Borise & Zientarski 2018; nothing opened here bears on that disagreement.

sources.quote: Lexical stress is weakly implemented in Georgian phonology. It is neither distinctive nor culminative (polysyllabic words are reported to have more than one stressed syllable). Although there is no general consensus in the literature as to the position of the stress in a word, the following rules of thumb are proposed by textbooks: (a) in bi- and trisyllabic words stress is initial, (b) in polysyllabic words, primary stress falls on the antepenultimate and secondary stress on the initial syllable (Robins and Waterson 1952, Aronson 1990: 18).
sources.locator: §2.2, p. 7 (draft pagination); also §5 p. 27 ('The first syllable and the antepenultima bear stress, whereby primary stress falls on the antepenultima') and §6 p. 32
sources.note: A focus-intonation study that adopts, from textbooks, the rule: initial stress in 2-3 syllable words, antepenult primary + initial secondary in longer words; it says stress cues are melodic, stressed syllables are not longer, and 'the phonetic realization of stress is postlexical in Georgian' (Zhgenti 1963's rhythmical group). This is the same pattern as the catalog rule string (antepenult primary, initial secondary), so it confirms the classification, but only as a second-hand rule of thumb; Borise 2023 later found no acoustic evidence for antepenultimate stress.

sources.note: Controlled production study (multiple speakers, words of 2-5 syllables in several phrasal contexts): fixed initial word stress cued by duration (and possibly intensity); F0 is phrasal (L pitch accent on initial syllable, phrase accent on penult, high final boundary tone); no evidence for antepenultimate stress. The catalog quotes only this paper's abstract sentence about F0; the body's placement finding (initial, not antepenult) contradicts the Gordon-2002 rule string while confirming the fixed, weight-insensitive kind.

sources.citation: Borise, Lena (2021). Focus projection need not be based on pitch accents: evidence from Georgian. Glossa: a journal of general linguistics 6(1): 128, 1-46.
sources.quote: The prosody of Georgian is relatively well-studied. The properties of word stress have long been debated, but there is consensus that (i) in di- and trisyllabic words stress is initial, and (ii) in longer words, in addition, secondary stress may occur on the antepenult or penult (Selmer 1935; Robins & Waterson 1952; Alkhazishvili 1959; Tevdoradze 1978). Experimental evidence demonstrates that Georgian has fixed initial stress, cued by greater duration as compared to other syllables/vowels (Vicenik & Jun 2014; Borise & Zientarski 2018; Borise 2019).
sources.note: A focus-projection study (CC BY; publisher site glossa-journal.org is behind an Anubis anti-bot wall, so the Internet Archive copy was used). States fixed initial stress cued by duration and measures initial ('stressed') syllable duration in subjects and objects under focus (Tables 12-14). Contradicts the catalog's antepenult rule string; consistent with the fixed, weight-insensitive kind.

sources.citation: [Not in target list; found via lingbuzz author search] Borise, Lena (2018, ms.). Tone and intonation in the languages of the Caucasus. lingbuzz/004204 (chapter ms; §3.2 'Georgian' surveys word-stress accounts, §4.2.2 instrumental studies).
sources.quote: It seems that the accounts that posit initial stress in shorter words and (ante)penultimate stress in longer words can be straightforwardly subsumed under a single account that posits antepenultimate stress. According to such an analysis, stress in disyllabic words, for the lack of an antepenultimate syllable, would target the initial syllable. Some evidence against this seemingly more economical analysis comes from a recent instrumental study, Borise & Zientarski (2018); see section 4.2.2.
sources.note: Survey of the whole Georgian literature (Tschenkeli 1958, Tevdoradze 1978: initial; Ioseliani 1840, Gorgadze 1912, Akhvlediani 1949, Gudava 1969: antepenult; Marr, Rudenko, Dirr, Janashvili, Aronson, Hewitt: syllable-count dependent; Zhghenti 1953/1963: rhythmic group), with tables of Zhghenti's and Robins & Waterson's results; concludes (p. 21) 'there is evidence for initial word stress in Georgian, cued by duration and easiest to identify in shorter words'. Refines: shows the catalog's antepenult rule is the 'economical' reading of the older literature and that the instrumental evidence goe…

sources.citation: Borise, Lena (2017). Prosody of focus in a language with a fixed focus position: Evidence from Georgian. In Aaron Kaplan et al. (eds.), Proceedings of the 34th West Coast Conference on Formal Linguistics (WCCFL 34), 89-96. Somerville, MA: Cascadilla Proceedings Project.
sources.quote: Georgian stress is acoustically weak – that is, in many cases, none of the syllables in a phonological word are perceptually more prominent than others. [...] There is a broad distinction between accounts that argue that the placement of stress depends on the syllable count, targeting the antepenult and /or one of the syllables closer to left edge of a phonological word (Robins & Waterson 1952; Aronson 1990; Skopeteas & Féry, to appear), and ones that argue that Georgian has fixed initial stress (Skopeteas et al. 2009; Vicenik & Jun 2014). Here, I adopt the initial-stress approach
sources.note: About the phrase accent L on the penult of the predicate as the prosodic marker of focus; only summarizes the word-stress debate (antepenult-by-syllable-count vs fixed initial) and adopts fixed initial stress, adding that 'nothing hinges on the analysis of lexical stress adopted here'. Documents that the catalog's antepenult rule is one of two competing accounts.

sources.quote: 'According to Tevdoradze (1978), primary stress always falls on the first syllable of a word. In polysyllabic words, secondary stress occurs. In four-syllable words, secondary stress falls on the second syllable from the end, in five-syllable words ... on the third syllable from the end, and in six-syllable words on the fourth syllable from the end'; analysed as left-to-right disyllabic trochees (déda-švìl-oba). Primary = initial, not antepenult.
